title: Pairwise stream interference - Nsight capture notes and mitigation ideas
content:
Goal:
Quick investigation notes from a targeted Nsight capture to test the hypothesis that pairwise interference between memcpy (async copy) streams and compute kernels at certain microbatch skews is driving intermittent tail-latency spikes on dedupe/rerank workloads.

Background/context:
- Symptoms reported: 99.9th token latency spikes (2–3x baseline) on some traffic mixes when sequence length and incoming microbatch arrival times are skewed. Not constant — shows up under specific arrival patterns and when running two logical streams (compute + high-frequency KV-prefetch copies).
- Recent changes: moved KV prefetch to a dedicated async copy stream (stream 3) to avoid blocking compute on stream 0. Observed regressions on mixed small/large requests after that change.

Hypotheses (short):
1) Pairwise interference: memcpy bursts on stream 3 create contention on shared DMA engine / L2 / copy engine scheduling and cause brief delays in kernel launch completion for stream 0 kernels (launch gap).
2) CUDA graph replay paths exacerbate launch gaps due to serialization points (graph replay reuses streams differently).
3) Microbatch skew (arrival jitter) lines up copies with hot kernel phases producing constructive interference and tail spikes.

Experiment setup:
- Instance: p4d-like testbed (8x A100-ish), single process pinned to GPU 0 for consistent trace.
- Workload: synthetic mix based on production prompt histogram: 60% short (<128), 30% mid (128–512), 10% long (>512).
- Trace tool: Nsight Systems 2024.3, sampling + timeline capture.
- Metrics collected: kernel launch timestamps, memcpy start/end, stream ids, SM active percentage, L2 BW, PCIe/NVLink transfer windows, nvprof-like metrics for kernel occupancy.
- Run variants: (A) baseline (prefetch on stream 0), (B) prefetch on stream 3 async, (C) same as B but with artificial jitter to microbatch arrivals to emulate skew, (D) B + cudaGraph replay enabled.

Commands used (representative):
- nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx -o capture_a --sample=cpu,os --duration=60 --force-overwrite --stop-on-exit --capture-range=kernel  \
  ./run_inference --workload=synthetic_mix --duration=60
- For kernel metrics: ncu --metrics sm__warps_active.avg,pct,achieved_occupancy --target-processes all --launch-skip 0 ./run_inference

Quick notes from captures (raw-ish observations):
- Variant A (baseline): launch gaps small and consistent, avg token latency stable. SM utilization moderate (55–68%), L2 BW steady. No obvious clustered memcpy bursts during critical decode loops.
- Variant B (async prefetch on stream 3): occasional clustered memcpy bursts overlap with decoder head phases. On those overlaps, we see a ~200–300 us extra gap between kernel enqueue and actual SM activity start; kernel launch appears queued but not executing. Tail latencies correlated with these overlap windows.
- Variant C (jittered arrivals): frequency of overlap increases and tail 99.9 jumps from ~20ms to ~48ms in one run. Nsight timeline shows memcpy on stream 3 occupying DMA engine for bursts of ~400us; immediately following, the expected kernel launch sits in the driver queue for ~180–350us before SM work starts.
- Variant D (cudaGraph replay): serialization points inside replayed graph appear to force ordering across streams in some GPU driver/hardware combos — observed longer stalls (~300–500us) vs B. Replay reduced CPU overhead but increased chance that memcpy and kernel launches contend at graph boundary.

Detailed timeline notes (examples):
- t=12.042s: memcpyHtoD(stream3) start 12.042s -> end 12.0424s (duration 400us)
- t=12.04245s: kernelA enqueue on stream0 (timestamped)-> SM activity not seen until 12.04275s (+300us gap)
- SM active ramp at 12.04275s with lower than expected achieved_occupancy for first 50us (cache warmup miss pattern observed)

Root-cause reasoning (working):
- The device-level DMA engine and internal copy engines have limited concurrency and can preempt or occupy resources that the scheduler needs to start kernels promptly (especially on architectures where copy engines share crossbar resources).
- When memcpy bursts are frequent and align with kernel enqueue windows, the driver/firmware introduces micro-serialization to maintain coherency; kernels end up queued even though host code already enqueued them.
- CudaGraph helps reduce host work but can worsen ordering semantics for mixed-stream ops depending on how graphs are constructed and replayed.

Immediate mitigation ideas (practical):
1) Stream shaping: throttle/pacing of prefetch copies so bursts are spread (token-bucket style) rather than big spikes aligned with decode. Implement client-side pacing in the prefetcher.
2) Copy priority/peer policy: experiment with cudaStreamAttachMemAsync / cudaStreamPriority (where supported) to lower prefetch priority relative to decode. Prioritize compute streams.
3) Small-copy coalescing: merge many small prefetch copies into fewer larger copies when possible to reduce overhead peaks.
4) Smart scheduling: if using cudaGraph, build graphs to avoid heavyweight copy nodes right next to kernel boundaries; consider separate replay groups and explicit synchronization fences where predictable.
5) Fallback path: detect microbatch skew patterns and temporarily move prefetch back onto compute stream (or serial path) during hot phases to avoid cross-stream interference.

Experiment follow-ups (next steps):
- Controlled microbench: isolate DMA engine occupancy by running synthetic memcpy bursts while measuring kernel launch latency (vary sizes, count, and stream IDs). Quantify threshold where median gap > 100us.
- Priority experiments: test cudaStreamCreateWithPriority and measure whether priority setting reduces observed gaps on our target HW.
- Graph construction variants: create two graph layouts (A: interleaved copy+compute nodes, B: grouped copies then grouped compute) and measure tail-latency under identical traffic.
- Telemetry: add fine-grained NVTX around prefetch and decode critical paths plus counters for memcpy byte counts per 100ms bucket so production traces can be scanned for alignment events.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How much of the effect is hw/firmware-specific (we saw stronger stalls on older driver/firmware on lab GPU vs newer driver where effect is muted). Need to sweep driver versions.
- Does NVLink vs PCIe topology change the shape of interference? Our lab machines use NVLink; customer VMs on PCIe might show different profiles.
- Are there kernel-side cache-warmup behaviors that amplify the apparent launch delay? Some of the early SM activity shows cache misses that could make short stalls appear larger.

Action items: (owners)
- Marcus: run copy-only microbench sweep and produce CSV with gap vs copy rate by 2025-10-10.
- Daniel: test cudaStream priority permutations + driver 525 vs 535 and report changes 2025-10-12.
- Aisha: prototype a pacing shim for the prefetcher (token bucket) and test with synthetic jittered arrival scenarios 2025-10-14.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally terse — raw captures attached to Confluence page. Looking for feedback on experiment design and whether to escalate to firmware/vendor (NVIDIA) if priority APIs don't help.
- Also consider whether this is a case for making prefetching opt-in per model profile, since not all models/seq-lengths suffer equally.

Attachments (local capture refs):
- nsight_capture_B_2025-10-03.qdrep (uploaded to shared folder)
- ncu_metrics_B_2025-10-03.txt

End of notes.
